summary: This MDN Web Docs page documents the JavaScript method Object.prototype.valueOf(), which converts an object's this value to an object and is meant to be overridden for custom type conversion. It explains that the base implementation is deliberately useless for primitive conversion, that valueOf is called in priority by numeric and primitive conversion while toString is preferred for string conversion, and that @@toPrimitive takes precedence over both. The page includes examples such as a custom Box class and unary plus behavior on various objects. The rest of the clipped page is navigation, sidebars and footer boilerplate, including a long list of standard built-in objects and related links.
one_line: MDN reference page on JavaScript's Object.prototype.valueOf() method, its role in type conversion, and overriding it for custom objects.
key_facts: The valueOf() method of Object instances converts the this value to an object and is meant to be overridden by derived objects for custom type conversion logic.
valueOf() takes no parameters and its return value is the this value converted to an object.
For valueOf to be useful during type conversion, it must return a primitive value.
Calling aPrimitiveValue.valueOf() generally does not invoke Object.prototype.valueOf(), because all primitive types have their own valueOf() methods.
Numeric conversion and primitive conversion call valueOf() in priority, while string conversion calls toString() in priority.
The Object.prototype.valueOf() base implementation is deliberately useless because by returning an object, its return value will never be used by any primitive conversion algorithm.
The @@toPrimitive method allows more control over the conversion process and will always be preferred over valueOf or toString for any type conversion.
In the Box class example, new Box(123) gives box + 456 equal to 579 and box == 123 equal to true.
Unary plus on new Date() returns the current timestamp, the same as new Date().getTime().
Unary plus on {} returns NaN, on [] returns 0, on [1] returns 1, on [1, 2] returns NaN, and on new Set([1]) returns NaN.
The specification reference is ECMAScript Language Specification, section sec-object.prototype.valueof.
